title: Egyptian medicine into Greece
summary: Greeks credited Egypt with deep medical wisdom, and one Hippocratic jaw technique matches a far older papyrus. How much they really borrowed is still argued.
body: Greeks long treated Egypt as the home of medicine. The *Odyssey* has Helen drugging wine with a gift from Polydamna, "a woman of Egypt," a land of potent herbs where everyone was said to be a skilled physician. In the sixth century BCE the Persian king Darius sent the Egyptian priest Udjahorresnet home to restore the "House of Life," a temple center of learning, so Egyptian medical teaching was still alive when Greeks were writing their first medical books.

Hard evidence of borrowing is thinner than the reputation. In 1930 the Egyptologist James Henry Breasted argued that the Hippocratic way of resetting a dislocated jaw is identical to the one in the Edwin Smith Papyrus, and a few remedies, such as the milk of a woman nursing a boy, turn up in both traditions. The closest contact came after Alexander: Herophilus taught and dissected at Alexandria under the first two Ptolemies. Whether Egyptian practice shaped what he did there is argued rather than shown.

confidence.note: That Greeks admired Egyptian medicine is plain from their own literature; specific borrowings rest on a handful of parallels such as Breasted's jaw-reduction match, which may reflect shared common sense rather than copying. Influence on Alexandrian anatomy is plausible but undocumented.

title: Babylonian medicine into Greece
summary: Babylon had a vast, organized medical literature centuries before Hippocrates. Scholars see echoes in early Greek texts, but nobody has shown how ideas crossed.
body: Babylonian and Assyrian healers built a large, systematic medical literature long before the Greeks: a catalogue from Assur shows that Mesopotamia had an organized corpus of medicine more than two centuries before Hippocrates. Greeks on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor lived within reach of that world, and Assyriologists such as Markham Geller have pointed to parallels between Akkadian medical texts and early Greek writings linked to the medical center of Cnidos.

A parallel is not a pedigree. The differences are deep: Babylonian medicine set out no explicit theory of humors or of hot against cold, and its recipes sit beside incantations, while the Hippocratic writers argued from nature. Geller himself stresses how Babylonian practice differed from its Greek counterpart. Influence by trade, travel or Persian-era contact is plausible, but it remains a hypothesis built on resemblances, not a documented transfer.

confidence.note: The age and scale of Mesopotamian medicine are well established from cuneiform tablets; the claim that it shaped Hippocratic medicine rests on suggestive parallels in a few texts, with no direct evidence of transmission.

title: Greek medicine into Arabic
summary: In Abbasid Baghdad, translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq turned Galen and Hippocrates into Syriac and Arabic, giving Islamic medicine its Greek foundation.
body: From the middle of the eighth century to the end of the tenth, caliphs, courtiers and wealthy physicians in Baghdad paid to have Greek science put into Arabic, often by way of Syriac, the language of the Christian scholars who did much of the work. The greatest translator was Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808–873), a Christian of the Church of the East who trained in Baghdad and served the caliph al-Mutawakkil. By his own count, ten years before his death he had made 95 Syriac and 34 Arabic versions of Galen alone.

Hippocratic treatises and Dioscorides' herbal followed, in several Arabic versions. The movement did more than preserve old books. It created a precise Arabic medical vocabulary and handed Galen's humoral medicine to physicians from Spain to Iran and India, who used it as the common framework for centuries of their own writing.

confidence.note: Surviving manuscripts, Hunayn's own account of his Galen translations and later bibliographies document the movement in unusual detail; scholars debate its motives more than its scale.

title: Indian medicine into Arabic
summary: Under the Barmakid viziers, Sanskrit classics by Charaka and Sushruta were put into Arabic and Indian physicians worked in Baghdad, a tributary later overshadowed by Greek.
body: Arabic medicine had an Indian tributary as well as a Greek one. Its patrons were the Barmakids, a family of Buddhist origin from Balkh who ran the Abbasid administration until their sudden fall in 803. Under the vizier Yahya ibn Khalid, Sanskrit classics, including the compendia of Charaka and Sushruta, were translated in Baghdad, some by way of Persian.

Later sources name an Indian physician, Manka, who came to Baghdad, treated the caliph Harun al-Rashid and stayed on to translate; Yahya is also said to have brought Indian doctors to work in a hospital he founded. A century later al-Razi was still quoting Indian authorities in his vast notebook, the *Hawi*. Much remains hazy. The best accounts come from biographers writing generations afterward, and historians admit they know relatively little about this side of the translation movement.

confidence.note: That Sanskrit medical works reached Arabic around 800 is accepted; details such as who translated what, and the Barmakid hospital, rest largely on al-Nadim's tenth-century Fihrist and similar later sources.

title: Arabic medicine into Latin
summary: From Constantine the African in Italy to Gerard of Cremona in Toledo, translators carried Arabic medicine, and the Greek medicine inside it, into Latin Europe.
body: Latin Europe first met Arabic medicine through Constantine the African, who in late eleventh-century Italy turned Arabic medical books into Latin, often disguising where they came from; his versions included Hunayn's Arabic *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates. In the twelfth century the center shifted to Toledo, newly in Christian hands and rich in Arabic manuscripts. There Gerard of Cremona (d. 1187) translated al-Razi's *Book for al-Mansur*, al-Zahrawi's surgery and Ibn Sina's *Canon*.

In 1279 Faraj ben Salim, a Sicilian-Jewish physician working for Charles of Anjou, put al-Razi's enormous *Hawi* into Latin as the *Continens*. These books, and the Greek medicine they carried, became the backbone of European medical teaching; the *Canon* was still read at Louvain and Montpellier in the seventeenth century.

confidence.note: The translators, their texts and many manuscripts survive and are well studied; exact dates for individual translations are often approximate.

title: Indian medicine into China
summary: Buddhist monks and texts carried Indian healing into China: tales of the physician Jivaka, recipes in his name and, many believe, needle surgery for cataract.
body: As Buddhism spread from India into China, healing traveled with doctrine. Monastic rules, sutras on illness and stories of the Buddha as physician were translated into Chinese. The legend of Jivaka, the Buddha's own doctor, famed for opening the skull, survives in Chinese versions from the fourth and fifth centuries, and the celebrated physician Sun Simiao later compiled formulas named after him. A Sanskrit and Khotanese medical text attributed to Jivaka turned up at Dunhuang on the Silk Road.

Eye surgery is the case most often cited. Couching, pushing a clouded lens out of the line of sight with a needle, is described in the *Sushruta Samhita*, and the technique has been traced from India to China and on to Japan. How deeply any of this reshaped mainstream Chinese medicine, rather than Buddhist circles, is still debated.

confidence.note: Indian medical material in Chinese Buddhist texts is well documented; the size of its influence on Chinese medical practice, and lineages such as cataract couching, are argued from scattered evidence and partly asserted.

title: Greek medicine back into Europe
summary: Byzantine manuscripts, humanist translators and the Aldine press gave Europe Galen and Hippocrates in their own Greek, and new Latin versions made from it.
body: Byzantine scholars who reached Italy around the fall of Constantinople in 1453 brought Greek manuscripts and the skill to read them. Humanist physicians wanted Galen and Hippocrates without the layers of medieval Latin and Arabic. The Englishman Thomas Linacre, who had worked with the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius and studied under Niccolò Leoniceno, published new Latin translations of Galen from 1517, replacing versions made from incomplete manuscripts. Scholars such as Janus Lascaris copied Galen from ninth-century Greek manuscripts in Florence.

Printing made the recovery permanent. The Aldine press issued Galen's complete works in Greek in 1525 and the first Greek edition of the Hippocratic corpus in 1526. The return to the sources had an ironic result: reading the genuine Galen closely made his mistakes easier to see, and within a generation anatomists were correcting him.

confidence.note: The editions, translators and manuscripts are documented in surviving books and catalogues; how much the Greek revival, rather than new dissection, drove the later break with Galen is a matter of interpretation.

title: American remedies into Europe
summary: Guaiac, tobacco, sarsaparilla, ipecac and above all cinchona bark crossed the Atlantic, popularized by books like Nicolás Monardes's 'Joyfull newes out of the newe founde worlde'.
body: Within decades of Columbus, American plants were entering European pharmacies. Guaiac wood was shipped from America in the sixteenth century as a supposed specific for syphilis, and tobacco, sarsaparilla and curare followed. Their great publicist was the Seville physician Nicolás Monardes, who never crossed the Atlantic but grew American plants and tried them on his patients. His book, first published in Spanish in 1565, appeared in Latin in 1574 and in English in 1577 as *Joyfull newes out of the newe founde worlde*.

The most consequential import was cinchona bark from the Andes, first documented in Spanish use in Peru around 1630; Andean peoples seem to have used it against shivering. Shipped to Europe by the Jesuits and known as Jesuit's powder, it became the standard treatment for intermittent fevers, which were shown two centuries later to be malaria. Ipecacuanha arrived in the same century. Where Indigenous healers' knowledge lay behind these drugs, European books rarely recorded it.

confidence.note: The arrival of these drugs is well documented in printed books; claims for many of them, guaiac especially, rested on hope rather than effect, and the Indigenous origins of the knowledge are usually inferred rather than recorded.

title: Ottoman inoculation into Europe
summary: Reports from Constantinople and Smyrna, and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's example, brought the Ottoman practice of smallpox inoculation to London.
body: In the Ottoman Empire, children were given a mild case of smallpox on purpose by putting matter from a smallpox sore into a small cut. In December 1713 the physician Emmanuel Timoni described the practice in a letter from Constantinople that was read to the Royal Society in May 1714; Giacomo Pylarini, a Padua-trained physician, published his own account in 1716. Timoni reported that Circassians and Georgians had brought the custom to Constantinople some forty years earlier.

Learned reports changed little until Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador, watched the old women who did the "engrafting" each autumn and had her son inoculated. Back in London during an epidemic, she had her daughter inoculated in April 1721, the first time it was done in Britain. That August an experiment on condemned prisoners at Newgate helped persuade the doubters.

confidence.note: Timoni's and Pylarini's reports, Montagu's letters and the 1721 London events are well documented; Montagu's personal influence is sometimes overstated relative to the physicians and royal patrons who took the practice up.

title: African inoculation into Boston
summary: An enslaved West African man, Onesimus, told Cotton Mather how he had been inoculated in Africa, setting off Boston's 1721 inoculation campaign.
body: In colonial New England the decisive informant was an enslaved man. Onesimus, given to the Puritan minister Cotton Mather by his Boston congregation in 1707, told Mather he had been through an operation in Africa that gave him a mild smallpox and lifelong protection. Mather questioned other Africans in Boston and heard similar accounts, which matched what he read of Constantinople in the Royal Society's *Philosophical Transactions*.

When smallpox struck Boston in 1721, Mather pressed for inoculation, and on 26 June the physician Zabdiel Boylston began with his own son and two enslaved members of his household, a man and a boy. Boylston's figures, published in London in 1726, counted 6 deaths among 282 people inoculated against 844 among 5,759 natural cases. African knowledge, recorded only through Mather's pen, set the experiment going.

confidence.note: Mather's letters and Boylston's published account document the episode well; everything known of Onesimus himself comes from Mather, and sources differ on whether he arrived in 1706 or 1707.
